comparator.name: Greek and Latin Language and Culture (Griekse en Latijnse taal en cultuur)
comparator.sourceNotes: The dated 2026–2027 guide identifies the UvA programme and verifies the early language courses and the thesis. The ordinary 180 EC curriculum assumes the regular language preparation; a compensating entry route is separate. The ACASA collaboration predates the joint degree beginning in 2027–2028. The guide identifies Dutch as programme language and course records confirm that some units are taught in English.

core: Cumulative Greek and Latin language acquisition, linguistics, translation and original-text reading
Greek and Latin literature, myth, epic, poetry, prose and literary interpretation
Ancient Greek and Roman cultures, Mediterranean history, material culture and source evaluation
Ancient philosophy and its intellectual traditions
Classical rhetoric, close reading, translation and the analysis of style
Reception of classical antiquity in later literature, culture and public memory
Humanities research, source criticism, academic writing and the bachelor thesis
adjacent: Material and archaeological study of the ancient Mediterranean
Ancient democracy, citizenship, empire and philosophy in later political and legal debate
Greek and Latin language, philology and original-text expertise
questions: How did classical antiquity shape later societies and political ideas?
How do classical texts and myths acquire new meanings across periods and media?
How did ancient communities organise power, citizenship, culture and conflict?

trace: examines the rise, organisation and fall of major empires, including Rome, and the theories used to explain imperial power
traces warfare in the western world from Greek hoplites and Roman legionnaires onward, covering the military organisation of the ancient societies studied in the cultural-history strand
develops source criticism and independent historical research through a modern history topic
introduces the Western philosophical tradition from the ancient Greeks onward, supplying the ancient philosophical material and the argumentative technique the programme builds on
works through virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism from their historical sources, including the ancient ethical theories read in the philosophy strand
examines how influential Western thinkers theorised human nature, society and political authority, beginning with the classical political philosophers
introduces the material culture of ancient societies from the Near East to classical Athens and Rome, reading artefacts and production techniques as evidence about the communities that made them
studies the archaeology of community and political decision-making in early-democratic Greece directly from its material remains
reconstructs how Athenian democracy was built and how it was expressed in myth, religion, art, literature and architecture, and traces how that heritage was later remembered
examines how a humanities discipline writes its own history and trains art-historical research, visual analysis and academic writing
compares ancient Greek and Roman myth and epic with other traditions and tests how narrative forms travel between cultures
develops practical criticism and literary interpretation, establishing the formal analysis of literary texts that the programme applies to classical material
surveys canonical literary works chronologically from the epic of Gilgamesh onward, including the ancient texts that shaped the Western literary tradition
analyses how literary texts are reworked in a different medium, giving concrete method for studying the afterlife of canonical narratives
uses contrasting interpretive theories in an independent literary research project
teaches classical rhetorical theory and practice from Plato, Aristotle and Quintilian and the construction of persuasive argument
uses grammatical and stylistic evidence to explain interpretive effects in literary and nonfiction texts
puts classical rhetorical theory into practice through public speaking, debate and storytelling in a community-engaged setting
extends classical rhetoric and argumentation theory into contemporary models of framing and persuasion across public discourse
combines lyric forms, performance and creative writing with reflection on inherited conventions
traces Western art from the early Renaissance onward, the period in which classical forms and subjects were deliberately revived, and trains visual analysis
studies Renaissance Italian art and its connections through Mediterranean and wider exchange, providing context for the later life of classical forms
analyses pre-digital media objects, including early printed books, and how their material properties shaped the production, circulation and preservation of knowledge
sets out legal, social and normative perspectives on law and surveys constitutional, criminal, international and private law, giving the legal vocabulary this programme needs
surveys the modern period from 1815, the era in which popular sovereignty, nationalism and classical political models were argued over in the terms the programme examines
examines human rights both as positive law and as a historical and philosophical construction, the modern counterpart of ancient arguments about who belongs to a political community
covers the sources of international law together with the use of force, armed conflict and refugee law, the contemporary legal frame for questions of movement and membership
compares how five constitutional orders establish government, sovereign powers and civil rights, giving the comparative method for reading ancient constitutional arrangements
compares property, tort and contract across contemporary legal systems as a supporting contrast in how societies organise rights and obligations
supplies the analytical tools for comparing political systems and explaining how they function and change
introduces the schools of international-relations theory and applies them to historical and contemporary cases of power between polities
examines how a composite political order exercises public authority and turns competing interests into policy
examines the causes and dynamics of violent and nonviolent conflict and the conditions for lasting peace across history, sociology, political science and law
trains qualitative research design, fieldwork and interpretive data analysis for studying how people make sense of their social and political world

alternatives.label: Classical antiquity through literature, rhetoric, philosophy & archaeology
alternatives.concept: Explore classical antiquity through literature in translation, rhetoric, ancient philosophy and archaeology. Study how myths, texts and visual traditions were reworked in later periods.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is organised around classical literature and myth, rhetoric, ancient philosophy, Greek archaeology, imperial history and the later reception of antiquity. The label states those related fields and does not imply Greek or Latin proficiency.
progression: First-year literature, rhetoric, philosophy and archaeology precede ancient history and reception. Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean follows Introduction to Western Art History in the fourth term. Rhetoric in Action follows its foundation in the sixth term.

alternatives.label: Antiquity, democracy & the politics of the present
alternatives.concept: Use ancient Athens as a case for studying citizenship, political participation and exclusion. Connect archaeology, political philosophy and imperial history with later debates about democracy, rights and law.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum uses archaeology, empire and ancient political philosophy as its starting point, then concentrates on law, comparative politics, international relations and modern historical research. The label reflects that question-led structure rather than presenting it as a Classics degree.
progression: Early philosophy, archaeology and the law gateway support later work on democracy, empire, rights, conflict and modern institutions. Renaissance art adds historical context for the transmission of classical culture. Formal prerequisites and offerings pass.
alternatives.distinctness: 11 courses and 82.5 EC differ in each direction. The first emphasises literature, rhetoric and reception. The second adds political institutions, comparative law and historical contexts to its central study of ancient democracy and citizenship.
traceOverrides: examines how Western thinkers from the classical political philosophers onward theorised political authority and the good community, which is the question this programme carries into the present
studies the archaeology of community and collective decision-making in early-democratic Greece, giving this programme its material evidence for how an ancient democracy actually worked

reconstructs how Athenian democracy was built, how ancient commentators attacked it as too inclusive and too emotional, and how that contested heritage has been reused since, which is this programme's central case
examines how empires rise, hold and lose power, placing Rome alongside later imperial formations that invoked it
shows how myths of political power, war and community travel and change across cultures
develops independent historical inquiry and source criticism through modern history, as a supporting method for evaluating later uses of the past
examines Renaissance Italian visual culture in Mediterranean and wider exchange, adding a historical context for the transmission of inherited forms

candidates.label: Antiquity, democracy and the politics of the present
Greek and Latin language, philology and original-text study
candidates.rationale: Current UCR courses offer classical literature in translation and historical and archaeological interpretation. No cumulative Greek or Latin acquisition, translation, linguistics or original-text sequence can be constructed.

selection.assessment: Two related-fields options have substantive foundations in classical antiquity. The first emphasises translated literature and reception. The second uses ancient democracy and citizenship to organise comparisons across periods. The ancient-language candidate lacks cumulative language and original-text study.

blocks: Greek and Latin language, linguistics & original texts
UCR offers no ancient Greek language acquisition or original-language reading sequence.
UCR offers no Latin language acquisition or original-language reading sequence.
UCR has no continuation course in Greek and Latin language acquisition and reading.
UCR has no advanced combined Greek and Latin language course in philosophical and rhetorical prose.
UCR has no Latin linguistics course.
UCR has no Greek linguistics course.
Both study classical literary genres and contextualise ancient texts. UCR includes epic and Greek tragedy in a much wider survey in translation.
Both study ancient epic, myth and interpretation. UCR compares Greek and other narrative traditions in translation; UvA requires close reading and translation of Homer.
Both require advanced humanities interpretation and independent written research; UCR provides a literary research project rather than a Classics term paper.
UCR reads Virgil in translation but has no Latin-language epic course.
UCR has no original-language course in late-antique and medieval Latin literature.
UCR has no original-language course in late-antique and medieval Greek literature.
UCR has no Latin lyric course in the original language.
UCR reads Greek tragedy in translation as part of a wider survey. UvA provides a dedicated Euripides, translation and reception course.
UCR develops creative practice and studies adaptation in separate courses. UvA combines this work specifically with the reception of Greek and Latin texts.
Ancient history, material culture & humanities research
Both study Rome and imperial power. UCR compares Roman and other empires; UvA also follows Hellenistic and Italian cultures through texts and material evidence.
Both teach source criticism through historical investigation. UCR applies it to modern history; UvA focuses on sources for classical antiquity.
Both interpret the ancient Near East and Greek world through cultural and material evidence; UCR embeds them in a global archaeological survey.
Both examine how ancient places and objects acquire later meaning. UCR studies the contested heritage of Athenian democracy.
Both examine humanities knowledge and disciplinary interpretation; UCR does so through the historiography and practice of art history.
UCR has no compulsory ACASA excursion or equivalent credited field component.
UCR has no dedicated Greek-and-Latin historiography course based on original-language texts.
Both introduce ancient philosophical arguments; UCR continues through the wider Western philosophical tradition.
Political, legal & social reception of antiquity
This is genuine approved profiling and has no fixed subject content to align.
The comparator requires an independent Greek and Latin Language and Culture thesis; UCR’s comparison-only optional research element is placed here.

notes.text: UvA develops Greek and Latin grammar, translation and close reading of original texts across the degree. The UCR options explore related questions through translated literature, archaeology, philosophy, history and politics.
UvA includes 30 EC of elective space, a field excursion and a 12-EC thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.

audience.programmeDescription: Greek and Latin Language and Culture at the University of Amsterdam combines study of both languages and their original texts with ancient history, philosophy and material culture.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR option focuses on classical literature in translation and the reception of antiquity. The second starts from ancient democracy and compares citizenship and political institutions across periods.
